states.name: Alabama
states.note: The state DOT publishes no time limit or overnight rule — the sign at the individual rest area is the law. A few of these states post 4–6 hour limits at some sites that never made it into a statewide rule.

states.name: Alaska
states.note: Limits are set per rest area — check the posted sign. Sleeping in the vehicle is standard practice.

states.name: Arizona
states.note: Camping and campfires are banned; nothing in the ADOT rules addresses vehicle sleeping. The sign at the specific rest area governs.

states.name: Arkansas
states.note: The state DOT publishes no time limit or overnight rule — the sign at the individual rest area is the law. A few of these states post 4–6 hour limits at some sites that never made it into a statewide rule.

states.name: California
states.note: Rest areas allow sleeping in the vehicle within the 8-hour cap. Tents, shelters and fires prohibited (21 CCR 2205).

states.name: Colorado
states.limit: No overnight parking or camping (posted sign)
states.note: The rule lives in the posted signs at every rest area rather than state code — but a posted sign is enforceable. Treat as a no.

states.name: Connecticut
states.note: The state DOT publishes no time limit or overnight rule — the sign at the individual rest area is the law. A few of these states post 4–6 hour limits at some sites that never made it into a statewide rule.

states.name: Delaware
states.note: The state DOT publishes no time limit or overnight rule — the sign at the individual rest area is the law. A few of these states post 4–6 hour limits at some sites that never made it into a statewide rule.

states.name: Florida
states.note: A 3-hour cap covers the safety nap, not a night. Commercial vehicles get 10.

states.name: Georgia
states.limit: No limit — sleeping is a named permitted use
states.note: The clearest statute in the country: 'normal, customary, and temporary use ... for purposes of resting, sleeping, eating' is what rest areas are for. Camping (tents, gear set up outside) is defined separately and banned (GA Code 32-6-6).

states.name: Hawaii
states.note: Hawaii has no interstate system and no conventional rest areas. Overnight stays are governed by county rules and private property — see the BLM/county guidance below.

states.name: Idaho
states.note: ITD allows vehicle sleeping within posted limits; camping is defined by the hookups it bans (awning, chairs, stove).

states.name: Illinois
states.note: Three-hour cap; sleeping on the grounds prohibited per compilations.

states.name: Indiana
states.note: The state DOT publishes no time limit or overnight rule — the sign at the individual rest area is the law. A few of these states post 4–6 hour limits at some sites that never made it into a statewide rule.

states.name: Iowa
states.note: The state DOT publishes no time limit or overnight rule — the sign at the individual rest area is the law. A few of these states post 4–6 hour limits at some sites that never made it into a statewide rule.

states.name: Kansas
states.note: The statute's own word: one night permitted.

states.name: Kentucky
states.note: Short cap — plan around it.

states.name: Louisiana
states.note: The state DOT publishes no time limit or overnight rule — the sign at the individual rest area is the law. A few of these states post 4–6 hour limits at some sites that never made it into a statewide rule.

states.name: Maine
states.note: The state DOT publishes no time limit or overnight rule — the sign at the individual rest area is the law. A few of these states post 4–6 hour limits at some sites that never made it into a statewide rule.

states.name: Maryland
states.note: Camping and overnight parking both prohibited (COMAR 11-04-07-11).

states.name: Massachusetts
states.note: The state DOT publishes no time limit or overnight rule — the sign at the individual rest area is the law. A few of these states post 4–6 hour limits at some sites that never made it into a statewide rule.

states.name: Michigan
states.limit: None today — 48-h cap + camping ban proposed
states.note: MDOT held a public hearing on proposed rules (Oct 2025) that would add a 48-hour cap and camping ban. Nothing in force yet.

states.name: Minnesota
states.note: Cap applies where posted.

states.name: Mississippi
states.note: The state DOT publishes no time limit or overnight rule — the sign at the individual rest area is the law. A few of these states post 4–6 hour limits at some sites that never made it into a statewide rule.

states.name: Missouri
states.note: The state DOT publishes no time limit or overnight rule — the sign at the individual rest area is the law. A few of these states post 4–6 hour limits at some sites that never made it into a statewide rule.

states.name: Montana
states.note: MDT allows resting within the limit; camping at designated rest areas only.

states.name: Nebraska
states.limit: No statewide cap — camping banned except designated sites
states.note: The statute bans camping; it says nothing about a person asleep in a parked vehicle (Neb. Rev. Stat. 39-312).

states.name: Nevada
states.note: Generous for a rest-area rule — effectively a night plus a long day (NAC 408-595).

states.name: New Hampshire
states.limit: No statewide cap — tents/ground sleeping banned
states.note: The ban targets tents and sleeping on the ground, not vehicle sleeping (RSA 236:58).

states.name: New Jersey
states.note: The state DOT publishes no time limit or overnight rule — the sign at the individual rest area is the law. A few of these states post 4–6 hour limits at some sites that never made it into a statewide rule.

states.name: New Mexico
states.note: One of the most permissive caps in the country.

states.name: New York
states.note: Night-time cap is 3 hours for passenger vehicles.

states.name: North Carolina
states.limit: No statewide cap — tents/structures banned; 4-h signs at some sites
states.note: Tents and structures prohibited; some individual rest areas post 4-hour limits that never made it into a statewide rule.

states.name: North Dakota
states.limit: No statewide cap — 'No Overnight Camping' signs
states.note: The sign bans camping (undefined) and says nothing about the person asleep in the driver's seat. In practice: sleep inside, stay low-key.

states.name: Ohio
states.note: Camping prohibited; unattended vehicles may be towed after 3 hours. An occupied vehicle is a different question.

states.name: Oklahoma
states.note: No statewide rest-area rule at all; posted signs govern.

states.name: Oregon
states.note: Sleeping in the vehicle allowed within the cap; camping prohibited (OAR 734-030-0010).

states.name: Pennsylvania
states.note: Prohibited acts include 'sleeping anywhere but in a legally parked vehicle' — inside the van you're fine, briefly (67 Pa. Code ch. 443).

states.name: Rhode Island
states.note: The state DOT publishes no time limit or overnight rule — the sign at the individual rest area is the law. A few of these states post 4–6 hour limits at some sites that never made it into a statewide rule.

states.name: South Carolina
states.note: The state DOT publishes no time limit or overnight rule — the sign at the individual rest area is the law. A few of these states post 4–6 hour limits at some sites that never made it into a statewide rule.

states.name: South Dakota
states.note: The statute says 'temporarily resting in any vehicle' is not camping at all — but the 3-hour cap still applies (SDCL 31-7-17).

states.name: Tennessee
states.note: No overnight parking; two-hour cap.

states.name: Texas
states.note: A full day in any rest area — among the most permissive caps (Tex. Transp. Code 545.411). Tents/shelters prohibited.

states.name: Utah
states.note: UDOT tolerates extended vehicle stays; camping by sign is prohibited.

states.name: Vermont
states.limit: No statewide cap — camping banned unless designated
states.note: Overnight camping banned unless at a designated site; parking itself not addressed (23 V.S.A. 1325).

states.name: Virginia
states.note: Overnight parking itself is banned, not just camping. No sleeping in the buildings either.

states.name: Washington
states.note: Sleeping in the vehicle allowed within the cap (RCW 47.38.020).

states.name: Washington DC
states.note: Most DC streets ban overnight parking; check posted signs. Plan on a hotel or out-of-state rest area for long hauls through the capital region.

states.name: West Virginia
states.note: The state DOT publishes no time limit or overnight rule — the sign at the individual rest area is the law. A few of these states post 4–6 hour limits at some sites that never made it into a statewide rule.

states.name: Wisconsin
states.limit: No statewide cap — camping banned after notice
states.note: Camping prohibited after notice; vehicle sleeping not addressed (Wis. Stat. 89.13).

states.name: Wyoming
states.limit: Sleep in the vehicle — nothing set up outside
states.note: The state's own rest-area brochure tells you to sleep in the vehicle; don't pitch a tent or run out the slides.
